value.name: Component render and reconciliation cycle
steps: component receives props and reads state
component produces JSX or React nodes
React computes a virtual UI representation
reconciliation compares new and previous representations
React DOM applies required changes to the live DOM
value.mechanism: Declarative components specify the UI for a state; reconciliation computes the live DOM changes required to reflect the new output.

value.name: Props and state relationship
steps: child renders from props and local state
value.mechanism: Props carry values across component boundaries; state is internal component data that can influence the view.

value.name: Rules of Hooks
steps: call Hooks only at top level
call Hooks only from React function components or custom Hooks
keep call order consistent across renders
use linting to detect many violations
value.mechanism: Stable call order lets React associate Hook state and behavior with the correct call positions.

value.name: React Server Component flow
steps: server output passes data or JSX to client components
client component supplies browser interactivity when needed
value.mechanism: Server Components access server data sources and avoid shipping corresponding component JavaScript for client hydration; Client Components handle browser behavior.

value.name: Server-side rendering and hydration distinction
steps: server renders component tree into initial HTML
client React may take over and attach event handlers
value.mechanism: SSR supplies pre-rendered HTML for early display; hydration establishes client-side React behavior. The source distinguishes this from Server Components, which do not undergo hydration for their own output.

value.name: Flux unidirectional data-flow loop
steps: user interaction or event creates action
updated state propagates to view through props
value.mechanism: Actions describe events; stores change in response and views receive updated state, maintaining downward data flow and upward actions.

value.name: Class component lifecycle resource management

value.name: JSX compilation pipeline
steps: React executes component code and renders output
value.mechanism: JSX is a syntax extension that resembles HTML but is converted to JavaScript during compilation.

work can be spread across multiple frames

value.distinction: React focuses on UI and rendering; routing, networking, storage and other application-level capabilities may come from additional libraries or frameworks.
Props are values passed between components; state is internal component data.
Function components can use Hooks; class components use React.Component lifecycle methods. Classes remain supported, while functions are recommended for new components in the source.
Hooks expose state/effect and other capabilities to function components; lifecycle methods are used by class components.

SSR sends rendered HTML to the browser and may be followed by hydration; the source says Server Components execute only on the server and do not send corresponding JavaScript for client hydration of their output.
Server Components execute on the server and can access server-side data; Client Components provide browser-side interactivity and event handlers.
The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation used for comparison; the browser DOM is the live document updated with computed differences.
Rendering produces a UI representation; reconciliation compares representations to determine necessary live DOM changes.
JSX resembles HTML but is a JavaScript syntax extension transformed during compilation; it is not itself HTML markup sent unchanged to the browser.
React supplies the UI library; React Router and Next.js provide routing and broader application-level features.
Flux is an architecture with actions, dispatcher, stores and views; Redux is a later state-management library often organized around a single store.
The source characterizes React's pattern as props flowing down and actions flowing up, contrasted with AngularJS's bidirectional flow.
Fiber segments work across frames; Stack is the older renderer described as less suited to complex dynamic changes in one chunk.
Server Components are server-executed UI components; Server Functions are asynchronous server-executed functions callable from Client Components.
The source describes an earlier BSD-plus-patent arrangement that caused controversy, followed by a 2017 MIT relicensing; the MIT license remains after foundation transfer.
CVE identifiers describe disclosed issues; remediation is tied to specific fixed or backported React versions in the source.
The source describes error boundaries as a React component type that catches JavaScript errors in a child tree and renders fallback UI.
SSR can let the browser display UI before client JavaScript has fully downloaded and executed; client hydration may then attach handlers for interactive UI.

value.question: What problem is React primarily designed to solve?
value.answer: Build component-based user interfaces and manage their rendering.

value.question: How does declarative UI differ from imperative programming in the source?
value.answer: The developer describes the view for a state; React updates it when data changes.

value.question: What are components?
value.answer: Reusable modular UI entities arranged in layers.

value.question: How do props differ from state?
value.answer: Props are passed between components; state is internal component data.

value.question: What does React DOM do?
value.answer: Renders components into a root element in the browser DOM.

value.question: What is the Virtual DOM?
value.answer: An in-memory UI representation used in comparison between renders.

value.question: What is reconciliation?
value.answer: Comparing new and prior UI representations to compute necessary live DOM updates.

value.question: What is JSX?
value.answer: A JavaScript syntax extension resembling HTML that is transformed into JavaScript.

value.question: What is a function component?
value.answer: A JavaScript function returning JSX or other React nodes.

value.question: What is a class component?
value.answer: An ES6 class extending React.Component and using lifecycle methods.

value.question: Why were Hooks introduced?
value.answer: To let function components access state and lifecycle-related features without classes.

value.question: What are the two Rules of Hooks?
value.answer: Call Hooks only at the top level and only from React functions/custom Hooks.

value.question: Why must Hook call order remain stable?
value.answer: The React Hook model relies on consistent call order across renders.

value.question: What does useState do?
value.answer: Manages component-local state.

value.question: What does useEffect do?
value.answer: Manages side effects.

value.question: What does useReducer do?
value.answer: Manages state transitions through a reducer, including local Redux-like patterns.

value.question: What is a custom Hook?
value.answer: Reusable stateful logic shared between components without changing component hierarchy.

value.question: What are React Server Components?
value.answer: Function components that execute exclusively on the server.

value.question: How do Server Components differ from SSR?
value.answer: Server Components do not send corresponding component JavaScript for hydration of their own output; SSR sends rendered HTML and may be hydrated.

value.question: What is hydration?
value.answer: Browser React takes over server-rendered UI and attaches event handlers.

value.question: What are Server Functions?
value.answer: Asynchronous functions executed on the server and callable from Client Components.

value.question: Does React include built-in routing?
value.answer: The source says it does not include a full-fledged routing solution out of the box.

value.question: What does React Router provide?
value.answer: Routes, navigation and URL-change handling.

value.question: What is SSR's initial-display benefit?
value.answer: The browser can display server-rendered HTML before client JavaScript has fully downloaded and executed.

value.question: What is Flux?
value.answer: A unidirectional data-flow architecture using actions, dispatcher, stores and views.

value.question: What does a Flux action describe?
value.answer: What happened, for example one user following another.

value.question: What does the dispatcher do?
value.answer: Routes actions to stores.

value.question: How does Redux relate to Flux?
value.answer: Redux is a later state-management library commonly using a single store as a source of truth.

value.question: What is React Fiber?
value.answer: An internal rendering architecture that segments work across frames.

value.question: What did React 16 introduce according to the source?
value.answer: Error boundaries, among other release changes.

value.question: What changed in React 18?
value.answer: Concurrent renderer, automatic batching and SSR support with Suspense.

value.question: What did React 19 introduce according to the source?
value.answer: Actions, Server Components support and improvements to static site generation.

value.question: What does unidirectional data flow mean in the article's shorthand?

source_claims.claim: React is a front-end JavaScript library focused on component-based user interfaces and rendering rather than a complete application library.
Developers describe the view for each application state and React updates the UI when data changes.
Components are modular and reusable; props carry values between components and state is internal component data.
Hooks allow function components to access state and lifecycle-related React features and must follow call-order rules.
Server Components execute exclusively on the server, can access server data sources and do not undergo client hydration for their own output.
React does not include a full routing solution out of the box; external libraries and frameworks provide routing and other application features.
React compares virtual UI representations and updates computed differences in the live DOM.
Server-side rendering sends initially rendered UI as HTML so the browser can display it before client JavaScript has fully downloaded and executed.
Flux expresses unidirectional flow through actions, a dispatcher, stores and views; props carry updated state back to views.
React was created by Jordan Walke, first deployed internally in 2011, used at Instagram in 2012 and open-sourced in May 2013.
React Fiber replaced the older Stack rendering algorithm with segmented work that can be spread across multiple frames.
The source records React Server Components vulnerabilities disclosed in late 2025 and lists fixed versions.
React was relicensed under MIT in 2017 after controversy about an earlier patent clause and remained MIT-licensed after the 2026 foundation transfer.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: React focuses on UI and rendering; routing, networking, storage and other application-level capabilities may come from additional libraries or frameworks.
Props are values passed between components; state is internal component data.
Function components can use Hooks; class components use React.Component lifecycle methods. Classes remain supported, while functions are recommended for new components in the source.
Hooks expose state/effect and other capabilities to function components; lifecycle methods are used by class components.

SSR sends rendered HTML to the browser and may be followed by hydration; the source says Server Components execute only on the server and do not send corresponding JavaScript for client hydration of their output.
Server Components execute on the server and can access server-side data; Client Components provide browser-side interactivity and event handlers.
The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation used for comparison; the browser DOM is the live document updated with computed differences.
Rendering produces a UI representation; reconciliation compares representations to determine necessary live DOM changes.
JSX resembles HTML but is a JavaScript syntax extension transformed during compilation; it is not itself HTML markup sent unchanged to the browser.
React supplies the UI library; React Router and Next.js provide routing and broader application-level features.
Flux is an architecture with actions, dispatcher, stores and views; Redux is a later state-management library often organized around a single store.
The source characterizes React's pattern as props flowing down and actions flowing up, contrasted with AngularJS's bidirectional flow.
Fiber segments work across frames; Stack is the older renderer described as less suited to complex dynamic changes in one chunk.
Server Components are server-executed UI components; Server Functions are asynchronous server-executed functions callable from Client Components.
The source describes an earlier BSD-plus-patent arrangement that caused controversy, followed by a 2017 MIT relicensing; the MIT license remains after foundation transfer.
CVE identifiers describe disclosed issues; remediation is tied to specific fixed or backported React versions in the source.
The source describes error boundaries as a React component type that catches JavaScript errors in a child tree and renders fallback UI.
SSR can let the browser display UI before client JavaScript has fully downloaded and executed; client hydration may then attach handlers for interactive UI.

misconceptions.misconception: React includes a full routing and application stack by itself.
misconceptions.correction: The source says React focuses on UI/rendering and relies on external libraries or frameworks for routing and other application capabilities.

misconceptions.misconception: Props and state mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Props are passed between components; state is internal to a component.

misconceptions.misconception: Hooks can be called inside class components.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly says Hooks do not work inside classes.

misconceptions.misconception: Hooks may be called inside conditions or loops.
misconceptions.correction: Hooks should be called at the top level so call order remains stable across renders.

misconceptions.misconception: React Server Components are simply another name for server-side rendering.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes them: Server Components execute on the server and do not ship corresponding component JavaScript for client hydration of their own output.

misconceptions.misconception: React only supports browser execution.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes SSR, Server Components and Server Functions in addition to client rendering.

misconceptions.misconception: The Virtual DOM is the browser's live DOM.
misconceptions.correction: The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation compared during reconciliation; React applies computed changes to the live DOM.

misconceptions.misconception: Every UI update replaces the entire live DOM.
misconceptions.correction: The source says React computes differences and updates only the parts of the live DOM that need changing.

misconceptions.misconception: JSX is just HTML embedded in JavaScript.
misconceptions.correction: JSX is a JavaScript syntax extension that resembles HTML and is transformed into JavaScript during compilation.

misconceptions.misconception: Class components are no longer supported.
misconceptions.correction: Class components remain supported, although the source recommends function components for new components.

misconceptions.misconception: React Fiber changed the syntax developers write.
misconceptions.correction: The source says Fiber changed internal execution/rendering algorithms, not the React programming syntax.

misconceptions.misconception: Every form of server-rendered React output necessarily hydrates the same way.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes Server Components, whose output does not undergo client hydration, from SSR interactive UI that may be hydrated.

misconceptions.misconception: Using useReducer requires a centralized Redux store.
misconceptions.correction: The source says useReducer can create reducer-based state local to a component without a centralized store.

misconceptions.misconception: React has always been distributed under MIT.
misconceptions.correction: The source documents Apache 2.0 at initial release, BSD plus patent text in 2014, and MIT from the 2017 release onward.

misconceptions.misconception: A vulnerability disclosure by itself means every deployed application is already fixed.
misconceptions.correction: The source lists specific fixed/backported versions; operators need to identify their installed versions and apply the relevant remediation.

misconceptions.misconception: A React component under Flux should directly mutate props passed to it.
misconceptions.correction: The source says components should not directly modify props; callbacks create actions sent through the dispatcher to update stores.

questions.question: What problem is React primarily designed to solve?
questions.answer: Build component-based user interfaces and manage their rendering.

questions.question: How does declarative UI differ from imperative programming in the source?
questions.answer: The developer describes the view for a state; React updates it when data changes.

questions.question: What are components?
questions.answer: Reusable modular UI entities arranged in layers.

questions.question: How do props differ from state?
questions.answer: Props are passed between components; state is internal component data.

questions.question: What does React DOM do?
questions.answer: Renders components into a root element in the browser DOM.

questions.question: What is the Virtual DOM?
questions.answer: An in-memory UI representation used in comparison between renders.

questions.question: What is reconciliation?
questions.answer: Comparing new and prior UI representations to compute necessary live DOM updates.

questions.question: What is JSX?
questions.answer: A JavaScript syntax extension resembling HTML that is transformed into JavaScript.

questions.question: What is a function component?
questions.answer: A JavaScript function returning JSX or other React nodes.

questions.question: What is a class component?
questions.answer: An ES6 class extending React.Component and using lifecycle methods.

questions.question: Why were Hooks introduced?
questions.answer: To let function components access state and lifecycle-related features without classes.

questions.question: What are the two Rules of Hooks?
questions.answer: Call Hooks only at the top level and only from React functions/custom Hooks.

questions.question: Why must Hook call order remain stable?
questions.answer: The React Hook model relies on consistent call order across renders.

questions.question: What does useState do?
questions.answer: Manages component-local state.

questions.question: What does useEffect do?
questions.answer: Manages side effects.

questions.question: What does useReducer do?
questions.answer: Manages state transitions through a reducer, including local Redux-like patterns.

questions.question: What is a custom Hook?
questions.answer: Reusable stateful logic shared between components without changing component hierarchy.

questions.question: What are React Server Components?
questions.answer: Function components that execute exclusively on the server.

questions.question: How do Server Components differ from SSR?
questions.answer: Server Components do not send corresponding component JavaScript for hydration of their own output; SSR sends rendered HTML and may be hydrated.

questions.question: What is hydration?
questions.answer: Browser React takes over server-rendered UI and attaches event handlers.

questions.question: What are Server Functions?
questions.answer: Asynchronous functions executed on the server and callable from Client Components.

questions.question: Does React include built-in routing?
questions.answer: The source says it does not include a full-fledged routing solution out of the box.

questions.question: What does React Router provide?
questions.answer: Routes, navigation and URL-change handling.

questions.question: What is SSR's initial-display benefit?
questions.answer: The browser can display server-rendered HTML before client JavaScript has fully downloaded and executed.

questions.question: What is Flux?
questions.answer: A unidirectional data-flow architecture using actions, dispatcher, stores and views.

questions.question: What does a Flux action describe?
questions.answer: What happened, for example one user following another.

questions.question: What does the dispatcher do?
questions.answer: Routes actions to stores.

questions.question: How does Redux relate to Flux?
questions.answer: Redux is a later state-management library commonly using a single store as a source of truth.

questions.question: What is React Fiber?
questions.answer: An internal rendering architecture that segments work across frames.
